method: COMPILED FROM 2 SOURCES. S1: PARAPHRASED AND HASH-ANCHORED from National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) 'Generalised anxiety disorder and panic disorder in adults: management (CG113), section 1.3 Stepped care for people with panic disorder' (published 26 January 2011, last updated 15 June 2020, last reviewed 11 September 2026), 21 claims; LICENCE: © NICE. Terms of use 18.2: 'Except for personal use, study or personal research, copyright content owned by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) may not be used, reproduced, translated, distributed or transmitted in any form, in whole or in part ... without the prior written agreement of NICE.' (read at https://www.nice.org.uk/terms-and-conditions (section 18.2, use of NICE content outside the United Kingdom)). S2: QUOTED from Bandelow B, Werner AM, Kopp I, Rudolf S, Wiltink J, Beutel ME, for the German S3 guideline panel (AWMF), European Archives of Psychiatry and Clinical Neuroscience 272:571-582 (doi 10.1007/s00406-021-01324-1) 'The German Guidelines for the treatment of anxiety disorders: first revision' (published online 6 October 2021 (English summary of the German S3 guideline, version 2, 2021)), 14 claims; LICENCE: CC BY 4.0 (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> element for PMC8490968). Verify each source separately: verify.py --source <file> --only-source S<n>. Edition 2.0 adds S2, the English summary of the German S3 anxiety-disorder guideline (2021), because no current Australian panic-disorder guideline is readable: the RANZCP 2018 guideline remains archived ('reference use only'), and searches of Europe PMC and Australian Prescriber found no Australian replacement. The S1 claims and anchors are unchanged. Table rows appended with pmc_text.py --append-tables (2026-09-24); claims from S2 Table 1 (ICD-10 descriptions of panic disorder and agoraphobia) and Table 4 (antidepressant adverse effects). S2 Tables 3 and 5 have merged cells and Table 6 is an image, so they were not extracted.

claims.claim: **Take a full history:** the person's background, whether they self-medicate, and any cultural or personal factors that will shape care. No self-report screening tool is validated well enough to recommend, so rely on consultation skills.
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), 'Generalised anxiety disorder and panic disorder in adults: management (CG113), section 1.3 Stepped care for people with panic disorder', published 26 January 2011, last updated 15 June 2020, last reviewed 11 September 2026, https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg113/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Expect comorbidity, especially depression and substance misuse.** Before an SSRI, ask about cocaine use (interactions) and do not stack serotonergic drugs.
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), 'Generalised anxiety disorder and panic disorder in adults: management (CG113), section 1.3 Stepped care for people with panic disorder', published 26 January 2011, last updated 15 June 2020, last reviewed 11 September 2026, https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg113/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Agree with the person which problem to treat first**; a timeline of when each problem began helps set priorities among comorbidities.
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), 'Generalised anxiety disorder and panic disorder in adults: management (CG113), section 1.3 Stepped care for people with panic disorder', published 26 January 2011, last updated 15 June 2020, last reviewed 11 September 2026, https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg113/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **A single panic attack is not panic disorder.** In the emergency department, chest pain is more likely to be panic disorder when coronary disease is absent and the person is female or relatively young.
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), 'Generalised anxiety disorder and panic disorder in adults: management (CG113), section 1.3 Stepped care for people with panic disorder', published 26 January 2011, last updated 15 June 2020, last reviewed 11 September 2026, https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg113/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **What panic disorder looks like (S2, ICD-10 F41.0):** sudden anxiety attacks with physical symptoms such as palpitations, sweating, tremor, dry mouth, breathlessness, a choking feeling, chest pain, abdominal discomfort, unreality and pins and needles; attacks can come out of the blue, and many people then avoid places where they fear one. **Agoraphobia (F40.0)** is fear of places that would be hard or embarrassing to leave during an attack, such as crowds, public transport or lifts; fear of being alone is common, and a companion may ease it.
claims.source_text: [Table 1] Anxiety disorders: short description according to ICD-10 classification [] [Table 1 row 1] Anxiety disorder: Panic disorder F41.0 · Description: Anxiety attacks of sudden onset, with physical manifestations of anxiety (e.g., palpitations, sweating, tremor, dry mouth, dyspnea, feeling of choking; chest pain; abdominal discomfort; feelings; feeling of unreality, paresthesia, etc.) Panic attacks can arise out of the blue; however, many patients start to avoid situations in which they fear that panic attacks might occur [Table 1 row 2] Anxiety disorder: Agoraphobia F40.0 without panic disorder F40.00 with panic disorder F40.01 · Description: Fear of places where it might be difficult or embarrassing to escape if a panic attack should occur (crowds, on public transport, or in closed spaces, e.g., elevators). Fear of being alone is also common. The presence of a companion may reduce anxiety
claims.locator: Bandelow B, Werner AM, Kopp I, Rudolf S, Wiltink J, Beutel ME, for the German S3 guideline panel (AWMF), European Archives of Psychiatry and Clinical Neuroscience 272:571-582 (doi 10.1007/s00406-021-01324-1), 'The German Guidelines for the treatment of anxiety disorders: first revision', published online 6 October 2021 (English summary of the German S3 guideline, version 2, 2021), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8490968/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Panic attack in the emergency department:** ask whether they are already being treated, do only the minimum tests needed to exclude an acute physical cause, usually do not admit, and refer back to primary care with written information explaining why.
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), 'Generalised anxiety disorder and panic disorder in adults: management (CG113), section 1.3 Stepped care for people with panic disorder', published 26 January 2011, last updated 15 June 2020, last reviewed 11 September 2026, https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg113/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Acute panic attack:** calm explanation that the attack is not a sign of serious illness is usually enough. Emergency medication is rarely needed; only in severe cases may lorazepam 1.0–2.5 mg (melting tablet) be given as needed.
claims.source_text: Only in rare cases, emergency drug treatment is an option in treating acute panic attacks. Mostly, talking calmly with the patient and explaining that the attack is not due to a serious medical condition is sufficient. Only in severe cases, lorazepam 1.0-2.5 mg melting tablets may be given p.r.n.
claims.locator: Bandelow B, Werner AM, Kopp I, Rudolf S, Wiltink J, Beutel ME, for the German S3 guideline panel (AWMF), European Archives of Psychiatry and Clinical Neuroscience 272:571-582 (doi 10.1007/s00406-021-01324-1), 'The German Guidelines for the treatment of anxiety disorders: first revision', published online 6 October 2021 (English summary of the German S3 guideline, version 2, 2021), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8490968/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Consider admission** for suicidality, chronic anxiety that has not responded to standard outpatient treatment, or marked comorbidity (major depression, personality disorder, substance misuse).
claims.source_text: Indications for hospitalization include suicidality, chronic anxiety disorders unresponsive to standard outpatient treatments, or marked comorbidity, e.g., with major depression, personality disorders or substance abuse.
claims.locator: Bandelow B, Werner AM, Kopp I, Rudolf S, Wiltink J, Beutel ME, for the German S3 guideline panel (AWMF), European Archives of Psychiatry and Clinical Neuroscience 272:571-582 (doi 10.1007/s00406-021-01324-1), 'The German Guidelines for the treatment of anxiety disorders: first revision', published online 6 October 2021 (English summary of the German S3 guideline, version 2, 2021), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8490968/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **CBT has by far the best evidence;** in phobic disorders, exposure to feared situations is a key ingredient. Psychodynamic therapy is weaker and should be offered only if CBT failed or is unavailable, or the informed patient prefers it.
claims.source_text: Of all psychological interventions, cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) has by far the best body of evidence. In the case of phobic disorders, confronting the patients with their feared situations in exposure sessions is a crucial ingredient of the therapy. … According to the guideline, patients with PDA, GAD, or SAD should be offered PDT only if CBT was shown to be ineffective or is unavailable, or if the adequately informed patient expresses a preference for PDT.
claims.locator: Bandelow B, Werner AM, Kopp I, Rudolf S, Wiltink J, Beutel ME, for the German S3 guideline panel (AWMF), European Archives of Psychiatry and Clinical Neuroscience 272:571-582 (doi 10.1007/s00406-021-01324-1), 'The German Guidelines for the treatment of anxiety disorders: first revision', published online 6 October 2021 (English summary of the German S3 guideline, version 2, 2021), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8490968/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Internet-based programs should not be used alone:** they can bridge a wait for face-to-face therapy or add self-help to standard therapy. There is not enough evidence for virtual-reality exposure in panic disorder.
claims.source_text: Therefore, the committee decided that IPIs should not be used as monotherapy but can be used to bridge a waiting period until face-to-face psychotherapy is available, or as an add-on self-help measure accompanying standard psychotherapy or medication treatment. … For PDA, there are not enough studies to support the use of VR.
claims.locator: Bandelow B, Werner AM, Kopp I, Rudolf S, Wiltink J, Beutel ME, for the German S3 guideline panel (AWMF), European Archives of Psychiatry and Clinical Neuroscience 272:571-582 (doi 10.1007/s00406-021-01324-1), 'The German Guidelines for the treatment of anxiety disorders: first revision', published online 6 October 2021 (English summary of the German S3 guideline, version 2, 2021), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8490968/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Psychotherapy and medication can be started together:** S2 finds no evidence for a fixed order. If one modality does not work well enough, switch to the other.
claims.source_text: The guideline does not recommend to start with psychotherapy before considering pharmacotherapy or vice versa, as there is no evidence from clinical studies justifying such a stepwise approach. As more data favor the combination of both modalities than not, both can be started at the same time. If response to psychotherapy or pharmacotherapy is insufficient, treatment should be switched to the other modality.
claims.locator: Bandelow B, Werner AM, Kopp I, Rudolf S, Wiltink J, Beutel ME, for the German S3 guideline panel (AWMF), European Archives of Psychiatry and Clinical Neuroscience 272:571-582 (doi 10.1007/s00406-021-01324-1), 'The German Guidelines for the treatment of anxiety disorders: first revision', published online 6 October 2021 (English summary of the German S3 guideline, version 2, 2021), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8490968/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Exercise (running 5 km three times a week) helps panic disorder only as an add-on;** it was less effective than clomipramine.
claims.source_text: Exercise (running 5 km three times a week) was shown to be effective in treating PDA [, ]. However, exercise was less effective than clomipramine and no more effective than a control condition, relaxation. Therefore, exercise can only be recommended as add-on treatment to standard treatments.
claims.locator: Bandelow B, Werner AM, Kopp I, Rudolf S, Wiltink J, Beutel ME, for the German S3 guideline panel (AWMF), European Archives of Psychiatry and Clinical Neuroscience 272:571-582 (doi 10.1007/s00406-021-01324-1), 'The German Guidelines for the treatment of anxiety disorders: first revision', published online 6 October 2021 (English summary of the German S3 guideline, version 2, 2021), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8490968/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Mild to moderate panic disorder: start with low-intensity help,** either self-help alone or self-help with facilitator support. Offer information on support groups and discuss exercise.
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), 'Generalised anxiety disorder and panic disorder in adults: management (CG113), section 1.3 Stepped care for people with panic disorder', published 26 January 2011, last updated 15 June 2020, last reviewed 11 September 2026, https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg113/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Moderate to severe panic disorder, with agoraphobia or without it: consider referral for CBT,** or for an antidepressant when the problem is long-standing or psychological treatment has been refused or has not helped.
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), 'Generalised anxiety disorder and panic disorder in adults: management (CG113), section 1.3 Stepped care for people with panic disorder', published 26 January 2011, last updated 15 June 2020, last reviewed 11 September 2026, https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg113/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **How to deliver CBT:** by trained, supervised therapists who stick to evidence-based protocols; 7 to 14 hours in total, usually as weekly sessions of 1 to 2 hours, finished within 4 months.
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), 'Generalised anxiety disorder and panic disorder in adults: management (CG113), section 1.3 Stepped care for people with panic disorder', published 26 January 2011, last updated 15 June 2020, last reviewed 11 September 2026, https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg113/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Brief CBT** should total about 7 hours and be built around structured self-help materials and focused tasks.
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), 'Generalised anxiety disorder and panic disorder in adults: management (CG113), section 1.3 Stepped care for people with panic disorder', published 26 January 2011, last updated 15 June 2020, last reviewed 11 September 2026, https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg113/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Do not prescribe benzodiazepines for panic disorder** (worse long-term outcome), and do not use sedating antihistamines or antipsychotics either.
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), 'Generalised anxiety disorder and panic disorder in adults: management (CG113), section 1.3 Stepped care for people with panic disorder', published 26 January 2011, last updated 15 June 2020, last reviewed 11 September 2026, https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg113/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Antidepressants are the only drugs for longer-term treatment.** SSRIs, SNRIs and tricyclics all have supporting evidence.
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), 'Generalised anxiety disorder and panic disorder in adults: management (CG113), section 1.3 Stepped care for people with panic disorder', published 26 January 2011, last updated 15 June 2020, last reviewed 11 September 2026, https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg113/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Offer an SSRI first**, unless there is a reason not to. If an SSRI is unsuitable, or a 12-week course has not helped, imipramine or clomipramine can be considered.
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), 'Generalised anxiety disorder and panic disorder in adults: management (CG113), section 1.3 Stepped care for people with panic disorder', published 26 January 2011, last updated 15 June 2020, last reviewed 11 September 2026, https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg113/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **S2's first line is an SSRI or an SNRI;** clomipramine is second line for panic disorder (as effective, more side effects).
claims.source_text: First-line drugs for anxiety disorders include the selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRI) and the serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRI) (Table 3). Drug side effects are listed in Table 4. For panic disorder, the tricyclic antidepressant clomipramine may be a second-line option. The drug is as effective as the SSRIs and SNRIs but has more adverse effects.
claims.locator: Bandelow B, Werner AM, Kopp I, Rudolf S, Wiltink J, Beutel ME, for the German S3 guideline panel (AWMF), European Archives of Psychiatry and Clinical Neuroscience 272:571-582 (doi 10.1007/s00406-021-01324-1), 'The German Guidelines for the treatment of anxiety disorders: first revision', published online 6 October 2021 (English summary of the German S3 guideline, version 2, 2021), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8490968/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Common adverse effects (S2 table):** SSRIs and SNRIs cause jitteriness, nausea, restlessness, headache, fatigue, appetite and weight change either way, tremor, sweating, sexual dysfunction, diarrhoea or constipation; SSRIs also QTc prolongation and SNRIs urinary problems. Tricyclics cause anticholinergic effects, drowsiness, dizziness, cardiovascular effects, weight gain, nausea, headache and sexual dysfunction. Check the product information for the full list.
claims.source_text: [Table 4 row 1] Medication class: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) · Side effects: Jitteriness, nausea, restlessness, headache, fatigue, increased or decreased appetite, weight gain, weight loss, tremor, sweating, QT C prolongation, sexual dysfunction, diarrhoea, constipation, and other side effects [Table 4 row 2] Medication class: Selective serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor (SNRI) · Side effects: Jitteriness, nausea, restlessness, headache, fatigue, increased or decreased appetite, weight gain, weight loss, tremor, sweating, sexual dysfunction, diarrhoea, constipation, urination problems, and other side effects [Table 4 row 3] Medication class: Tricyclic antidepressants (TCA) · Side effects: Anticholinergic effects, somnolence, dizziness, cardiovascular side effects, weight gain, nausea, headache, sexual dysfunction, and other side effects … [Table 4 footnote] Only most common and relevant side effects included. For details, see the current summary of product characteristics
claims.locator: Bandelow B, Werner AM, Kopp I, Rudolf S, Wiltink J, Beutel ME, for the German S3 guideline panel (AWMF), European Archives of Psychiatry and Clinical Neuroscience 272:571-582 (doi 10.1007/s00406-021-01324-1), 'The German Guidelines for the treatment of anxiety disorders: first revision', published online 6 October 2021 (English summary of the German S3 guideline, version 2, 2021), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8490968/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Benzodiazepines (S2):** advised against because of abuse potential, although effective. In exceptional cases (such as severe heart disease, suicidality or contraindications to standard drugs) they may be used for a limited time after weighing risks and benefits.
claims.source_text: The guideline group advised against the use of benzodiazepines because of their abuse potential, despite their high effectiveness in treating anxiety. However, in exceptional cases (e.g., severe cardiac disease, suicidality, contraindications for standard medications, and other conditions), benzodiazepines can be used for a limited time period after their risks and benefits have been weighed carefully.
claims.locator: Bandelow B, Werner AM, Kopp I, Rudolf S, Wiltink J, Beutel ME, for the German S3 guideline panel (AWMF), European Archives of Psychiatry and Clinical Neuroscience 272:571-582 (doi 10.1007/s00406-021-01324-1), 'The German Guidelines for the treatment of anxiety disorders: first revision', published online 6 October 2021 (English summary of the German S3 guideline, version 2, 2021), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8490968/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Improve adherence at the start:** warn that antidepressants take about 2 weeks to work (range 1–6 weeks) and may cause early jitteriness; start at half the usual dose; give the dose in the morning or at midday to avoid insomnia.
claims.source_text: Patients starting treatment with antidepressants (SSRIs, SNRIs, and TCAs) should be advised that these drugs generally take effect after a latency period of about 2 weeks (range 1-6 weeks). During the first weeks of treatment, some patients have a tendency to discontinue treatment with SSRIs and SNRIs due to initial jitteriness and nervousness. Compliance can be improved by informing patients about these potential adverse effects and by starting at half of the usually recommended dose. The drugs should be given in the morning or at midday to avoid insomnia which may occur during the first treatment weeks.
claims.locator: Bandelow B, Werner AM, Kopp I, Rudolf S, Wiltink J, Beutel ME, for the German S3 guideline panel (AWMF), European Archives of Psychiatry and Clinical Neuroscience 272:571-582 (doi 10.1007/s00406-021-01324-1), 'The German Guidelines for the treatment of anxiety disorders: first revision', published online 6 October 2021 (English summary of the German S3 guideline, version 2, 2021), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8490968/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Choosing the drug:** weigh age, past response, accidental and deliberate overdose risk (highest with tricyclics), tolerability, interactions, the person's preference, and cost where drugs work equally well.
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), 'Generalised anxiety disorder and panic disorder in adults: management (CG113), section 1.3 Stepped care for people with panic disorder', published 26 January 2011, last updated 15 June 2020, last reviewed 11 September 2026, https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg113/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Warn before starting:** side effects, including a short-lived rise in anxiety early on; a delayed onset of benefit; and withdrawal symptoms if doses are missed, reduced or stopped suddenly. Give written information.
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), 'Generalised anxiety disorder and panic disorder in adults: management (CG113), section 1.3 Stepped care for people with panic disorder', published 26 January 2011, last updated 15 June 2020, last reviewed 11 September 2026, https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg113/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Start low and titrate slowly;** doses at the top of the range are sometimes needed. Once the person improves, keep going for 6 months or more from reaching the best dose, then taper.
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), 'Generalised anxiety disorder and panic disorder in adults: management (CG113), section 1.3 Stepped care for people with panic disorder', published 26 January 2011, last updated 15 June 2020, last reviewed 11 September 2026, https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg113/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **No improvement after 12 weeks:** switch to an antidepressant from the other class, if a drug is still appropriate, or to another form of therapy.
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), 'Generalised anxiety disorder and panic disorder in adults: management (CG113), section 1.3 Stepped care for people with panic disorder', published 26 January 2011, last updated 15 June 2020, last reviewed 11 September 2026, https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg113/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **S2's switching rule is earlier:** no response after 4–6 weeks, change to a second standard drug; partial response after 4–6 weeks, first consider a higher dose. Add psychotherapy when medication is not working.
claims.source_text: In patients who are unresponsive to medications, the addition of psychotherapy is generally recommended. If there is no response to the first drug after 4-6 weeks of treatment, a second standard drug should be given instead. In case of a partial response after 4-6 weeks, raising the dose can be considered first.
claims.locator: Bandelow B, Werner AM, Kopp I, Rudolf S, Wiltink J, Beutel ME, for the German S3 guideline panel (AWMF), European Archives of Psychiatry and Clinical Neuroscience 272:571-582 (doi 10.1007/s00406-021-01324-1), 'The German Guidelines for the treatment of anxiety disorders: first revision', published online 6 October 2021 (English summary of the German S3 guideline, version 2, 2021), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8490968/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Continue medication for 6 to 12 months after remission** (longer after a long, recurrent or severe course), then taper slowly to avoid discontinuation symptoms.
claims.source_text: it is advisable to continue drug treatment for 6 to 12 months after remission has occurred. In patients with a long history of recurrent and/or severe anxiety symptoms, longer treatments may be necessary. To avoid discontinuation syndromes, the dose should be slowly tapered at treatment termination.
claims.locator: Bandelow B, Werner AM, Kopp I, Rudolf S, Wiltink J, Beutel ME, for the German S3 guideline panel (AWMF), European Archives of Psychiatry and Clinical Neuroscience 272:571-582 (doi 10.1007/s00406-021-01324-1), 'The German Guidelines for the treatment of anxiety disorders: first revision', published online 6 October 2021 (English summary of the German S3 guideline, version 2, 2021), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8490968/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Older people and pregnancy:** in older patients, allow for greater sensitivity to side effects and interactions (anticholinergic effects, orthostatic hypotension, ECG changes, falls, paradoxical reactions to benzodiazepines). In pregnancy, SSRIs generally compare favourably with the risks of untreated anxiety; when breastfeeding, consider CBT instead of medication.
claims.source_text: In older patients, an increased sensitivity to drug side effects and interactions has to be considered, including anticholinergic effects, risk of orthostatic hypotension and electrocardiogram changes, risk of falling, and paradoxical reactions to benzodiazepines. … However, the current evidence suggests that the use of many antidepressants, especially the SSRIs, is favorable compared to exposing the mother to the risks of untreated depression or anxiety disorders … Likewise, a careful assessment of the risk/benefit balance has to be done when a mother is breastfeeding. In such cases, CBT should be considered as an alternative to medication treatment.
claims.locator: Bandelow B, Werner AM, Kopp I, Rudolf S, Wiltink J, Beutel ME, for the German S3 guideline panel (AWMF), European Archives of Psychiatry and Clinical Neuroscience 272:571-582 (doi 10.1007/s00406-021-01324-1), 'The German Guidelines for the treatment of anxiety disorders: first revision', published online 6 October 2021 (English summary of the German S3 guideline, version 2, 2021), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8490968/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Stopping:** reduce the dose gradually over a long period. Common withdrawal symptoms are dizziness, numbness and tingling, nausea and vomiting, headache, sweating, anxiety and poor sleep. If they are severe, restart the drug (or a longer-acting one of the same class) and taper more slowly.
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), 'Generalised anxiety disorder and panic disorder in adults: management (CG113), section 1.3 Stepped care for people with panic disorder', published 26 January 2011, last updated 15 June 2020, last reviewed 11 September 2026, https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg113/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Refer to specialist mental health services after 2 interventions** (any mix of psychological therapy, medication or bibliotherapy) if significant symptoms remain.
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), 'Generalised anxiety disorder and panic disorder in adults: management (CG113), section 1.3 Stepped care for people with panic disorder', published 26 January 2011, last updated 15 June 2020, last reviewed 11 September 2026, https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg113/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Specialist reassessment** covers previous treatments and adherence, substance use (nicotine, alcohol, caffeine, recreational drugs), comorbidities, daily functioning, social networks, ongoing stressors and agoraphobic avoidance, with a full risk assessment and plan.
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), 'Generalised anxiety disorder and panic disorder in adults: management (CG113), section 1.3 Stepped care for people with panic disorder', published 26 January 2011, last updated 15 June 2020, last reviewed 11 September 2026, https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg113/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Review a new medicine within 2 weeks, then at 4, 6 and 12 weeks.** At 12 weeks decide whether to continue or change; if continuing, review every 8 to 12 weeks.
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), 'Generalised anxiety disorder and panic disorder in adults: management (CG113), section 1.3 Stepped care for people with panic disorder', published 26 January 2011, last updated 15 June 2020, last reviewed 11 September 2026, https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg113/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **People on self-help** should have primary-care contact, probably every 4 to 8 weeks, and progress should be tracked with short self-rated questionnaires (for example, the agoraphobic mobility inventory's panic subscale).
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), 'Generalised anxiety disorder and panic disorder in adults: management (CG113), section 1.3 Stepped care for people with panic disorder', published 26 January 2011, last updated 15 June 2020, last reviewed 11 September 2026, https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg113/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-23
